lede: Rotation week: Dow +1.1% Thursday as money left tech; hot PPI but 10y fell to 5.10%; Asia bounced; futures flat to slightly higher.

Thu close after Huang defense; still ~-15% on week (Investopedia, CNBC)
Thu; Deutsche Bank upgrade to buy, PT $136 (Investopedia)

geo_headlines: ROTATION, NOT RETREAT. Thursday the Dow rose 1.08% (550 points) as money moved out of tech into health care (+2.5%), Nike (+6%), Walmart and Home Depot; energy fell 1.6% and tech 1.1% (Investopedia). S&P 500 +0.33% to 7,744.06, 0.96% below its October 6 record close; Nasdaq 100 -0.05%, about 4% below its record; chips -0.88%. **CoreWeave closed up about 6% after Nvidia's Jensen Huang said its "cost of capital is actually decreasing" (AFP).**

HOT PPI, STRONG SPENDING. September producer prices rose 1.3% on the month vs 0.6% expected and 6.3% from a year ago vs 5.5%, the largest annual gain since 2022; core PPI 5.0%. Almost half the jump in goods for immediate demand traced to diesel (CNBC). Retail sales rose 0.8% vs 0.4% expected. The 10-year still fell to 5.10% (Treasury), from 5.19%.

BONDS' BEST WEEK SINCE FEBRUARY. The 10-year is 5.09% Friday morning and yields are headed for their biggest weekly decline since February (Bloomberg). The 2-year closed at 4.77%, the 30-year at 5.43%. FedWatch, as of Thursday 10/15: October hike 25.5% (from 29.9%), December 89.0%. Gold $4,198.70 (+0.7%).

WARSH: AI 'MOST CONSEQUENTIAL CHANGE'. At the IMF-World Bank meetings in Bangkok, Fed Chair Warsh called AI the most consequential change to the global economy in his lifetime, with a "bumpy" path (AFP). He said central bankers everywhere hear the same about "the surge in prices" and would not say what he will do at the remaining meetings; the FOMC meets October 27-28 (Investing.com).

ASIA BOUNCES; KOSPI WORST WEEK SINCE 2008. Nikkei +1.4% to 65,324.29 and Kospi +2.1% to 5,668.05 after Thursday's 4.9% and 7.6% drops; Jakarta fell more than 11%, its worst day since 1998 (AFP). The Kospi is still down 14.5% this week, its worst since October 2008 (CNBC). China urged state funds to buy shares (Bloomberg). Futures: S&P 7,804 (+0.17%), Nasdaq 100 30,123.25 (-0.07%).

OIL: WTI CATCHES UP TO BRENT. November WTI settled $97.97 (+3%) Thursday while December Brent slipped to $105.92, as cheaper US shipping lifted demand for US barrels (Rigzone). Now WTI $96.01 (-2.0%), Brent $106.15 (+0.2%). Hormuz flows are 68% of normal (Kpler); the US may ease sanctions on some shadow-fleet tankers to cut freight rates, and the IEA is releasing 20 million barrels of diesel (Reuters).

TODAY: IMPORT PRICES, OUTPUT, OPEX. 8:30 AM: import and export prices (BLS), consensus +0.9% and +1.0%. 9:15 AM: industrial production, +0.4% expected; capacity use 76.5%. Monthly options expiration. Houthis say they will keep targeting Saudi airports and oil sites; Riyadh's airport was attacked 20 times in October (coalition). Citizens Financial EPS $1.41, up 34%.
client_frame_short: This was a rotation week, not a crash. Money came out of the AI and chip stocks that had led for months and went into health care, consumer names and bonds. **The Nasdaq 100 is down about 3% since Monday and Korea had its worst week since 2008, yet the Dow is up about 1% for the week and bonds are on track for their best week since February.** That is exactly what a diversified portfolio is built to do. Inflation is still running hot, so the Fed stays on alert, but long-term plans do not need to change.
client_frame:
If a client calls this morning, the story is a market rotating, not a market breaking.

What happened this week: worries about how AI data centers get financed, plus hot inflation reports, knocked the AI and chip stocks that led for most of the year. The Nasdaq 100 fell about 3% since Monday, chip stocks are about 21% below their June peak, and Korea, home of Samsung and SK Hynix, had its worst week since 2008.

Where the money went: health care, consumer companies and bonds. Thursday the Dow rose 550 points while Nike, Eli Lilly, Walmart and Home Depot rallied. The 10-year Treasury yield fell from 5.19% to 5.10% in a day, and bonds are headed for their best week since February. The S&P 500 is less than 1% below its October 6 record.

The inflation picture: wholesale prices rose 6.3% over the past year, the most since 2022, much of it diesel and energy from the Middle East conflict. Shoppers kept spending, with retail sales up 0.8%. That is why the Fed is still weighing another hike; the odds of an October move are about one in four, and a December hike is close to fully priced.

The Fed Chair's long view: Warsh called AI the most consequential economic change of his lifetime, positive over time but with a bumpy path. That is a fair description of this week.

Why it matters: concentrated AI and chip portfolios felt this; balanced portfolios mostly did not. Leadership rotations like this happen inside long bull markets, and the investors who get hurt are usually the ones who chase whatever just worked.

For clients: diversification is earning its keep, high-quality bonds still pay about 5% for a decade, and this is a reasonable moment to rebalance toward targets, not to abandon them. What would change the view: a 10-year close above 5.40% (Thursday 5.10%), a 30-year above 5.75% (Thursday 5.43%), or US strikes on Iran that keep Brent well above $105 (now $106.15).
